title: The Netflix Prize: $1 million, not deployed
summary: Netflix paid $1,000,000 in 2009 for a recommendation algorithm that beat its own by 10.06%. It later said the gains did not justify the engineering effort.

beats.say: Netflix paid one million dollars for an algorithm it did not deploy.

data.verdict: Per Netflix's own 2012 post, as reported

beats.say: In October two thousand six, Netflix opened a contest to improve its recommendations.
The grand prize needed ten percent better predictions than its own algorithm, Cinematch.
The training data held about one hundred million ratings.
Those came from about four hundred eighty thousand users, on seventeen thousand movies.
More than five thousand teams submitted entries.
The winner hit ten point oh six percent. A rival matched it, twenty minutes later.
Netflix later said the gains did not justify the engineering effort.
Most users were streaming by then, not renting discs.
A winning model still has to fit the product.

facts.claim: Netflix opened the contest in October 2006 with a $1,000,000 grand prize for a 10% improvement over its Cinematch algorithm
facts.note: Wikipedia, Netflix Prize: start October 2, 2006; $1,000,000; 10% improvement over Cinematch

facts.claim: The training set held 100,480,507 ratings from 480,189 users on 17,770 movies, and 5,169 teams made 44,014 submissions
facts.note: Wikipedia, Netflix Prize: dataset and submission counts

facts.claim: BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos won with a 10.06% improvement, and The Ensemble matched it but submitted 20 minutes later
facts.note: Wikipedia: winner announced September 18, 2009; RMSE 0.8567, 10.06% improvement; The Ensemble matched, BellKor's came 20 minutes earlier

facts.claim: Netflix said the accuracy gains did not seem to justify the engineering effort, and most users were streaming rather than renting DVDs
facts.note: BGR (April 13, 2012), based on a Netflix blog post: gains did not justify engineering effort; most users streaming rather than renting DVDs
